newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: World Bank steps up effort to help Slovak business.
newsitem.headline: World Bank steps up effort to help Slovak business.

text.p: The International Finance Corporation (IFC), the lending arm of the World Bank, on Monday stepped up its development help for the Slovak private sector.

IFC officials said its Small Entrepreneur Fund (SEF) project would extend loans to small and medium-sized businesses at a rate of between two to three percent over the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR).

"Under the SEF, the IFC usually extends loans of $100,000 to $2.5 million, but we can also consider larger investments outside the SEF programme," Georgina Baker, the IFC investment officer on Monday told a seminar in Bratislava.
She added the IFC had not set any upper limit for investment in Slovakia. "There is no ceiling, we will assess projects that fulfil our basic criteria."
The programme exists throughout post-Communist Europe but the IFC has so far made no direct investment in Slovakia.
IFC Prague representative Krysti Brice blamed slow progress and opaqueness in the privatisation process for delays in entering the Slovak market.
Baker said the IFC aim was to serve only as a lender of last resort in Slovakia. "But when we enter a country we send a signal to other foreign lenders to come in and invest."

Apart from direct investment, which can cover only up to 40 percent of the overall investment in a particular project, the IFC also offered to act as an intermediary between Slovak companies and foreign bankers.
The IFC also offers funds to Slovak banks which can be used as credits to local entrepreneurs, but it rules out loans for buying shares within the privatisation process.
The IFC said it was encouraging companies to launch or widen their export activities and earn foreign currencies to become independent of fluctuations of the foreign exchange markets.
The World Bank affiliate has participated in the form of direct investment, consultancy services or as a mediator in talks between firms and banks, in several post-communist European countries.
